transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-03-04 14:30 UTC
Duration: 45m
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Arjun Patel (Redwood SE), Evelyn Hart (Lancaster Head of ML), Tom Rivers (Platform Eng), Sasha Kim (CTO)

Summary:
Quick cost/unit economics discovery focused on per-token pricing, batching/caching levers, and tradeoffs between Hosted vs Dedicated vs Private (VPC). Customer has strict budget limits, heavy bursty inference for trading signals, and residency/KMS concerns. Agreed to run a benchmark and send pricing model.

Transcript:
00:00 - Maya Chen: hey everyone, thanks for—uh—joining, this is Maya from Redwood, i've got Arjun here from solutions eng, and we're excited to walk through cost economics, right?
00:14 - Evelyn Hart: yeah hi thanks, quick context: we run inference for quant signals — pretty bursty trading windows, peaks about 500 concurrent reqs for short windows, average request length is about 120 tokens and sometimes up to 1k for research queries. budget for inference is tight, we need to understand unit economics.
00:30 - Arjun Patel: got it, that helps. two big levers we usually look at: batching/caching and model selection/quantization. and then deployment mode matters — hosted per-token vs dedicated reserved capacity gives different unit cost profiles.
00:50 - Tom Rivers: quick question: what's the per-token hosted pricing and how does that compare to a dedicated pool? we run around 10M tokens/day on average but spikes are the problem.
01:05 - Maya Chen: short answer: hosted is simpler operationally, billed per token plus optional features; typical hosted per-token list for our curated models ranges, example, redwood-1-small at $0.0008/token for gen (note: prices vary), whereas dedicated is committed monthly and can get you 3-5x lower token cost depending on utilization and batching efficiency.
01:25 - Sasha Kim: 3-5x is a big range; can you explain assumptions? like what utilization and batching numbers?
01:40 - Arjun Patel: yeah, great — assumptive example: a dedicated GPU pool with continuous batching and KV/prefix cache for common prompts. If you get 60-70% GPU utilization and sustain efficient micro-batching (avg batch size 8-12 for our workload), your amortized cost/token drops dramatically. But if utilization is low —like 10-20%— the committed cost looks worse.
02:05 - Evelyn Hart: our pattern is weird: most of the day low volume, then two 30-min windows with very high RPS. so we care a lot about burst handling and whether we need burst capacity or autoscaling.
02:20 - Maya Chen: that's classic. options: 1) hosted with automatic routing and burst from shared capacity — you pay per-token and it's elastic but unit price is higher; 2) dedicated + burst credits — reserved capacity for baseline, plus burst to hosted or overflow to a cheaper region; 3) private VPC/on-prem — best for compliance but operational overhead and hardware cost.
02:45 - Tom Rivers: can dedicated autoscale fast enough for those 30-min bursts without paying for a huge reserve?
02:58 - Arjun Patel: autoscale can react, but spin-up time for large GPU processes matters. common approach: reserve baseline for steady state, use pre-warmed workers for bursts or route overflow to hosted. we have policies to keep latency SLOs during scale events. Also prefix/KV caching helps reduce tokens for incremental queries.
03:20 - Evelyn Hart: how do you measure token savings from KV cache?
03:32 - Arjun Patel: we instrument per-route token diffs in the console; typically if you have repeated prefixes or context reuse, you can see 20-60% token reduction depending on cache hit rate. in trading signals, if you re-run analyses with small deltas, KV cache is very effective.
03:52 - Sasha Kim: security stuff — we need KMS, SSO, SOC2, and control plane separation. how does pricing change if we want private?
04:05 - Maya Chen: private gets a platform licensing fee plus infra — it's not per-token in the same way, it's more a fixed platform cost plus infra. we provide KMS integrations, SAML SSO, audit logs. we can share SOC2 docs after.
04:20 - Evelyn Hart: budget number: internally we have a goal to keep inference dollars under $40k/month for prod. is that doable?
04:32 - Arjun Patel: depends on model and utilization. using a smaller quantized model and heavy batching/caching, it's often possible. for 10M tokens/day naive hosted could exceed that; with dedicated and 50-60% utilization costs drop. we should run a cost model with your actual traffic and prompt lengths.
05:00 - Tom Rivers: okay let's get into specifics — can you walk through a sample cost calc?
05:10 - Maya Chen: sure — quick baseline: hosted per-token example for redwood-1-medium: $0.0009/gen token (example). 10M tokens/day -> $9k/day -> ~270k/month, so definitely not within 40k. but if you run on dedicated with reserved GPUs and 60% util and batching improvements you might get to $0.03-$0.06 per 1k tokens effective, which for 10M/day becomes about (10M/1000)*0.045 = $450/day -> ~13.5k/month. that's rough math.
05:55 - Evelyn Hart: that delta is huge. but our problem is we only get the 10M during spikes, average daily tokens maybe 2M. so committed makes sense if we can smooth with caching and off-peak workloads.
06:15 - Arjun Patel: exactly — another pattern is hybrid: reserved for baseline (2-3 nodes), and then route spikes to hosted; or to a cheaper regional dedicated pool if latency tolerates. we can also do scheduled scale for known market open times.
06:35 - Sasha Kim: what's the risk of model quality regression if we quantize aggressively to save cost?
06:48 - Arjun Patel: quantization/INT4 can be great but depends on model. we provide quantization profiles and we recommend running evals on a holdout prompt set; quality regressions are model-dependent — we can provide recommended profiles per model to balance perf and quality.
07:05 - Tom Rivers: do you support function-calling and streaming? that impacts tokens and latency.
07:15 - Maya Chen: yes, streaming and function/tool calling supported. streaming can increase usage slightly because of incremental tokens, but reduces perceived latency. function-calling can reduce tokens if you avoid verbose free-form responses.
07:35 - Evelyn Hart: for the benchmark, we want it to include: baseline 2 nodes dedicated, a hosted run, and a dedicated + burst test. can you capture p99 latency and cost/token?
07:50 - Maya Chen: yes we can. Arjun will run the benchmark with your sample workload. we'll instrument p50/p95/p99, cost per generated token and inference throughput.
08:05 - Arjun Patel: i'll also enable KV caching for one run to show delta. quick note: cache effectiveness depends on prompt reuse; please share a representative sample.
08:20 - Evelyn Hart: i'll share sample prompts and traffic shape, anonymized.
08:25 - Sasha Kim: are there any vendor lock-in concerns if we go Dedicated with Redwood? we have internal policy about portability.
08:35 - Maya Chen: good question — model artifacts and configs are portable; for private we can do on-prem. Dedicated uses standard containerized runtime; we provide tooling to export configs. but some optimizations like our compiled kernels are Redwood-managed and may be tied to our infra. we'll document portability tradeoffs.
08:55 - Tom Rivers: what about GPU types? can you do A100 vs H100 and cost differences?
09:05 - Arjun Patel: yes, different hardware profiles matter. H100 gives better throughput and lower latency for some models, but cost per-hour is higher. our cost model will include hardware sensitivity so you can decide.
09:20 - Evelyn Hart: latency SLOs — we need 95th < 300ms for short inference (<=128 tokens) during bursts. can dedicated meet that?
09:34 - Arjun Patel: with pre-warmed workers and continuous batching optimized for short requests, yes. hosted can also meet that but may vary in heavy multi-tenant bursts; dedicated gives the most predictable p95.
09:52 - Maya Chen: i'll summarize: run benchmark (hosted vs dedicated baseline vs dedicated+burst), include KV caching test, and we'll produce a cost spreadsheet mapping per-token and monthly spend under different utilization assumptions.
10:05 - Evelyn Hart: timeline — can we get initial numbers next week?
10:12 - Maya Chen: yes we can aim for that. Arjun will kick off the runs once we get samples.
10:20 - (brief cross talk)
10:30 - Tom Rivers: security docs? we need SOC2, KMS integration detail, and network diagrams for VPC flows.
10:38 - Maya Chen: we'll send SOC2 and KMS integration docs; for VPC we'll schedule a follow-up with infra.
10:45 - Evelyn Hart: ok sounds good. one more question — how do you charge for burst to hosted from dedicated? is it just hosted per-token overlay?
10:53 - Arjun Patel: yes bursts routed to hosted are billed at hosted per-token rates for the overflow. some customers buy burst credits if they want predictable billing; we can include that in the cost model.
11:05 - Sasha Kim: can you include an example of end-to-end cost with and without cache savings, with numbers?
11:12 - Maya Chen: yes that will be in the spreadsheet.
11:20 - Recap & next steps:
11:22 - Maya Chen: action items: we'll send pricing deck and cost model, Arjun will run benchmarks with KV on/off, Evelyn will share prompts and traffic profile; schedule infra follow-up for VPC/KMS.
11:40 - Evelyn Hart: great, thanks everyone.
11:45 - Meeting end.

References shared during call: pricing deck (link placeholder), cost-model spreadsheet (link placeholder), SOC2 and KMS docs (link placeholder), benchmark harness repo (link placeholder).
